exam: A 9‑month‑old presents with fast breathing and chest indrawing; what is your immediate management plan — classify severity, start first‑line antibiotic, give oxygen, and arrange referral if danger signs appear.
How does the WHO clinical definition of pneumonia differ from radiographic criteria, and why is this important in a district hospital — emphasizes reliance on bedside signs when X‑ray is unavailable.

A child with HIV presents with cough and fever; which additional pathogens should you consider and how does this affect antibiotic choice — include TB, opportunistic bacteria, and need for broader coverage.
Explain why chloramphenicol is avoided as a first‑line agent for severe pneumonia in this setting — risk of aplastic anaemia and poor efficacy against common pneumococci.

A child on malaria treatment develops respiratory distress; how do you differentiate malaria‑associated pulmonary oedema from bacterial pneumonia — focus on malaria test, rapid onset after fever, and response to antimalarials.
What are the red‑flag signs that mandate urgent referral to a higher‑level facility — list hypoxaemia, severe indrawing with poor perfusion, inability to drink, convulsions, and shock.

Describe how you would interpret a normal chest X‑ray in a child with clinical pneumonia signs — explain that early disease may be radiographically occult and treatment proceeds based on clinical criteria.
A patient fails to improve after 48 h of oral amoxicillin; what are the next steps — reassess adherence, consider resistant bacteria, obtain cultures if possible, and switch to parenteral therapy.
ai.title: Childhood Pneumonia
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Pneumonia is an acute infection of the lung parenchyma in children. In low‑resource settings diagnosis relies on clinical signs and simple tools, while severity guides treatment and referral.

b: Cough or difficulty breathing + any of: fast breathing, chest indrawing, or danger signs
Fast breathing thresholds: >50 breaths/min (2‑12 mo), >40 (12‑59 mo), >30 (5‑12 yr)
sections.p: Pneumonia is defined as an acute infection of the lung tissue causing alveolar inflammation and consolidation. In children the WHO clinical case definition is used when chest radiography is unavailable.

t.b: Confirms consolidation or infiltrates; helps differentiate lobar vs interstitial patterns
Detects hypoxaemia; SpO₂ < 90 % indicates need for oxygen and possible referral

t.a: Nasopharyngeal swab for PCR (if lab exists)
t.b: Identifies viral vs bacterial aetiology; guides antibiotic stewardship

b: Non‑severe: cough/difficulty breathing + fast breathing only
Severe: any chest indrawing
Very severe: any danger sign (e.g., inability to drink, convulsions, SpO₂ < 90 %)
sections.p: The WHO classifies pneumonia into three severity levels that dictate management and referral.

b: Streptococcus pneumoniae – most common bacterial cause
Haemophilus influenzae type b – less common after vaccination
Respiratory syncytial virus – leading viral cause in infants
Influenza virus – seasonal peaks
Mycobacterium tuberculosis – consider in chronic cough, especially with HIV
Malaria‑associated pulmonary oedema – in children with severe malaria
sections.p: In East Africa the aetiology reflects local pathogen prevalence and host factors.

b: Infants: tachypnoea, nasal flaring, grunting, poor feeding
Toddlers: cough, fast breathing, chest indrawing
Older children: productive cough, pleuritic chest pain, fever
Danger signs: inability to drink, convulsions, lethargy, SpO₂ < 90 %
sections.p: Presentation varies with age and severity, but key features are reproducible at the bedside.
Use investigations that answer a specific clinical question; when unavailable, rely on bedside assessment.

t.b: Leukocytosis suggests bacterial infection; normal count does not exclude it
Identifies bloodstream pathogens; guides targeted therapy
Rules out malaria as a co‑trigger of respiratory distress
Detects immunosuppression that alters pathogen spectrum and prognosis

b: Persistent hypoxaemia (SpO₂ < 90 % despite oxygen)
Severe chest indrawing with poor perfusion
Pleural effusion or empyema (dullness, reduced breath sounds)
Septic shock – cold extremities, capillary refill > 3 s
Bronchiectasis risk after recurrent episodes
sections.p: Recognise early signs that herald rapid deterioration or long‑term sequelae.

b: First‑line antibiotic for non‑severe bacterial pneumonia: oral amoxicillin (covers S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae)
If severe/very severe: parenteral ampicillin or benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin (avoid chloramphenicol due to marrow toxicity)
Oxygen therapy to maintain SpO₂ ≥ 90 % (use nasal cannula or mask)
Hydration – oral rehydration solution or IV fluids if unable to drink
Bronchodilators only if wheeze suggests co‑existing asthma
Avoid routine macrolides unless atypical pathogen suspected or local resistance high
sections.p: Treat the aetiology, provide supportive care, and monitor for deterioration.

b: Re‑evaluate at 48–72 h; if no clinical improvement, reassess diagnosis and consider referral
Complete full antibiotic course even if symptoms improve
Vaccination: PCV, Hib, measles, influenza
Promote exclusive breastfeeding for infants, reduce indoor air pollution, and improve nutrition
sections.p: Ensure resolution and reduce future risk.

b: Bronchiolitis – wheeze dominant, usually in < 2 yr, no chest indrawing
Pulmonary TB – chronic cough, weight loss, night sweats, often HIV‑positive
Severe malaria with pulmonary oedema – history of fever, malaria test positive
Congestive heart failure – hepatomegaly, peripheral edema, cardiomegaly on X‑ray
Normal chest X‑ray does not exclude early pneumonia; rely on clinical signs
Leukocytosis may be absent in viral infection or early bacterial disease
Pulse oximetry can be falsely high in severe anemia; assess clinical cyanosis as well
